entry.title: End-to-End Latency Profiling on Neuron
entry.summary: End-to-end profiling of LLM inference on Neuron at three levels, the PyTorch profiler on the host, the Neuron system profile across executions, and neuron-profile inside a single NEFF.
entry.content:
Inference latency on Neuron can be measured at three levels. The PyTorch profiler records what the host CPU does, including framework code, input preparation, and the calls that dispatch work to the device. A Neuron system profile records runtime activity across the whole run, such as each model execution on a NeuronCore. neuron-profile records what happens inside the device during a single execution of a compiled model (NEFF). An investigation usually uses them in that order.

Choosing a profiler

The PyTorch profiler captures:

  • CPU activity, including PyTorch operators and framework overhead
  • Input preparation on the host
  • The duration of each call to the Neuron device, including the wait for the result
  • The split between context encoding, which processes the prompt, and token generation, which produces one token per step

The system profile captures:

  • Neuron Runtime API calls and the ML framework trace for the whole run
  • How device executions are spaced across the run and across NeuronCores
  • Idle gaps between executions

The device profile captures:

  • Activity inside one NEFF execution
  • Per-engine activity, DMA transfers, collectives and semaphores

When time to first token or per-token latency is higher than expected, the PyTorch profile shows whether the time goes to the host or the device. The system profile shows how device executions are spaced across the run and across NeuronCores, which exposes gaps, stalls and long tails that a single execution does not show. The device profile then explains a slow execution operator by operator.

Capturing a PyTorch profile

A minimal capture around a transformers-neuronx generation call:

from torch.profiler import profile, ProfilerActivity

# Warm-up run, excluded from the profile.
model.sample(input_ids=input_ids, sequence_length=input_length + output_size, top_k=1)

with profile(activities=[ProfilerActivity.CPU]) as prof:
    model.sample(
        input_ids=input_ids,
        sequence_length=input_length + output_size,
        top_k=1,
    )

prof.export_chrome_trace("torch_profile.json")

ProfilerActivity.CPU records the host-side operators. The warm-up call keeps one-time costs, such as loading the model onto the device and filling caches, out of the measurement. The exported file uses the Chrome trace JSON format.

Each call into the Neuron runtime appears in the trace as a host-side operator. In the transformers-neuronx traces used here, the call is named neuron::_parallel_executor_run, and its duration covers dispatching the work and waiting for the device to finish. Operator names can differ between SDK versions, so the names in the queries below should be checked against the trace first.

Viewing the PyTorch trace

Perfetto opens Chrome trace files directly in the browser and handles large traces better than the older chrome://tracing viewer. Each operator appears as a slice on a timeline. Hovering over a slice shows its duration, and selecting a range of slices shows aggregate statistics.

Querying the PyTorch trace with SQL

Perfetto loads the trace into a database and accepts SQL in its query tab. The slice table holds one row per slice, with the start time ts and duration dur in nanoseconds.

Duration of each device call. Dividing by 1e6 converts nanoseconds to milliseconds:

SELECT ts, dur / 1e6 AS duration_ms
FROM slice
WHERE name = 'neuron::_parallel_executor_run'
ORDER BY ts;

Context encoding latency. The first device call of a generation processes the prompt, so its duration approximates the context encoding latency:

SELECT dur / 1e6 AS context_encoding_ms
FROM slice
WHERE name = 'neuron::_parallel_executor_run'
ORDER BY ts
LIMIT 1;

Per-token latency. The time between the starts of two consecutive device calls is the latency of one generated token as the application sees it, including any host-side gap between calls. LAG() returns the previous row’s timestamp, and the first call has no predecessor:

SELECT (ts - LAG(ts) OVER (ORDER BY ts)) / 1e6 AS token_latency_ms
FROM slice
WHERE name = 'neuron::_parallel_executor_run'
ORDER BY ts;

Average token generation latency. Averaging the gaps and dropping the first row gives the mean per-token latency:

SELECT AVG(token_latency_ms) AS avg_token_latency_ms
FROM (
    SELECT (ts - LAG(ts) OVER (ORDER BY ts)) / 1e6 AS token_latency_ms
    FROM slice
    WHERE name = 'neuron::_parallel_executor_run'
)
WHERE token_latency_ms IS NOT NULL;

These queries assume one slice per device call. If several threads each record the call, the queries should filter on a single thread first. Percentiles are easiest to compute by exporting the query result and processing it with NumPy.

Capturing a system profile

In the PyTorch profile, each device call is a single host-side slice. A system profile, introduced with Neuron Profiler 2.0, records the Neuron Runtime API calls and the ML framework trace for the whole run on one timeline. It shows how runtime calls and device executions are spaced across the run, but not the instructions inside an execution.

The runtime captures a system profile for an unmodified application when two environment variables are set (Neuron Profiler 2.0 guide):

export NEURON_RT_INSPECT_ENABLE=1
export NEURON_RT_INSPECT_OUTPUT_DIR=./output
python run_inference.py

The capture covers the whole lifetime of the process and writes its files to the output directory. A PyTorch or JAX profiler context in the same script should write to the same directory, so that all profile data for the run stays together. The guide describes how to view the result.

Typical analyses of a system profile include:

  • The distribution of NEFF execution durations across the run
  • The gaps between consecutive executions, which include any host-side work between them
  • The time each NeuronCore spends waiting in collective operations
  • Executions that take much longer than the rest, which point to the source of long tails

Capturing a device profile

The PyTorch profile and the system profile show which NEFF execution is slow. neuron-profile shows what happens inside that execution:

neuron-profile capture -n file.neff -s profile.ntff

The capture runs the NEFF on the device and writes the trace to an NTFF file. Models that run across several NeuronCores need the multi-worker options described in the Neuron Profile user guide.

Viewing the device profile

The web viewer stores the processed trace in InfluxDB 2.x, which must be installed and initialized once on the instance. The user guide lists the installation steps. After that, the following command processes the profile and prints a local URL, usually on port 3001:

neuron-profile view -n file.neff -s profile.ntff

When the profile runs on a remote instance, SSH port forwarding makes the viewer reachable from a laptop:

ssh my-instance -L 3001:localhost:3001 -L 8086:localhost:8086

The viewer is then available at http://localhost:3001.

A worked example

Consider a generation of 100 tokens that takes 800 ms when the expected latency is 400 ms.

  1. PyTorch profile. Capture one generation after a warm-up run and open it in Perfetto.
  2. Context encoding. The context encoding query returns 150 ms. Context encoding accounts for less than a fifth of the total.
  3. Token generation. The average token latency query returns 6.5 ms. Over 100 tokens, token generation accounts for 650 ms, so it is the phase to investigate.
  4. Host or device. The durations of the token generation calls are close to the gaps between them, so little time is spent on the host between tokens. The time goes to the device.
  5. System profile. The token generation executions take about the same time on every NeuronCore, and each core spends a large share of every step waiting in collective operations. Most of each step goes to collectives, and no single core is slower than the rest.
  6. Device profile. A neuron-profile capture of the token generation NEFF shows which engines wait on DMA or collectives, which narrows the problem to specific operators.

Practices

Reuse the queries. Running the same SQL queries and scripts on every profile gives a record of normal values for a model, and a regression shows up as a departure from those values.

Exclude warm-up. The first execution includes one-time costs such as loading the model and filling caches. A warm-up run before the profiled run keeps these costs out of the measurement.

Script long traces. For long captures, scripted analysis with the Perfetto trace processor or a Python script over the system profile is faster than scrolling through a UI.

entry.title: Block KV Paged Attention in vLLM’s NKI Kernel
entry.summary: How vLLM’s NKI flash paged attention kernel reads a block KV cache on Neuron, from the block table and mask layout to vectorized DMA loads, online softmax and the cache update.
entry.content:
vLLM stores the KV cache in fixed-size blocks of tokens. Each request owns a list of blocks, recorded in a block table, and blocks can be shared between requests that start with the same prefix. This layout, introduced with PagedAttention, lets memory grow with the number of tokens actually in use, and it is the basis for automatic prefix caching and chunked prefill. An attention kernel for this layout has to read keys and values through the block table instead of from one contiguous buffer.

vLLM’s Neuron backend includes such a kernel, written in the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI): flash_paged_attention in vllm/attention/ops/nki_flash_attn.py. The code excerpts below come from that file at the linked commit.

Inputs and layout

The kernel signature lists the tensors it works on:

@nki.jit
def flash_paged_attention(
    query,          # (1, n_heads, d, seq_q)
    key,            # (1, n_kv_heads, d, seq_k)
    value,          # (1, n_kv_heads, seq_v, d)
    kv_cache,       # (2, num_blocks, n_kv_heads, block_size, d)
    block_tables,   # (num_active_blocks, )
    mask,           # (seq_q, num_active_blocks * block_size + seq_q)
    softmax_scale=None,
    mixed_precision=True,
    LARGE_TILE_SZ=2048,
    return_debug_tensors=False,
):

Four properties of this interface shape the rest of the kernel:

  • Continuous batching with a batch size of 1. The batch dimension is always 1. The tokens of all requests in a step are concatenated along the sequence dimension, so seq_q is the total number of new tokens in the step.
  • A flat block table. block_tables lists every cache block that any request in the step reads, in one array. It is not a per-request table.
  • A mask that encodes the requests. mask has one row per new token and one column per cached token plus one per new token. A token may attend to a cached position only if that position belongs to the same request. Each request’s prefix-cache hits and chunked-prefill history therefore appear as ordinary cached blocks in this mask.
  • A fused K/V cache. Keys and values share one tensor, with keys at index 0 and values at index 1 of the first dimension.

The kernel launches on a two-dimensional grid of batch and KV head. For grouped-query attention, each program handles one KV head and loops over the query heads that share it:

batch_id = nl.program_id(axis=0)
head_id = nl.program_id(axis=1)
...
q_h_per_k_h = h // k_h

The kernel asserts a head dimension of at most 128, which matches the 128 partitions of the on-chip SBUF memory.

Two passes over the keys

The kernel computes attention in two passes, both feeding the same online-softmax accumulators:

  1. A loop over the cached context, one tile of LARGE_TILE_SZ tokens (2,048 by default) at a time. These tiles use the mask and no causal structure.
  2. One pass over the new tokens of the step, using key and value directly and applying the causal mask.

The first pass looks like this, with the loads and indexing trimmed:

for large_k_tile_idx in nl.sequential_range(0, num_large_k_tile):
    load_kv_tile_from_cache(cur_k_tile, cur_v_tile, kv_cache,
                            block_tables_sbuf, large_k_tile_idx, ...)
    for i in nl.affine_range(n_tile_q):
        cur_mask = nl.load(mask[nl.ds(i * B_P_SIZE, B_P_SIZE),
                                nl.ds(large_k_tile_idx * LARGE_TILE_SZ,
                                      LARGE_TILE_SZ)])
        for i_q_h in nl.affine_range(q_h_per_k_h):
            ...
            _flash_attention_core(q_tile, cur_k_tile, cur_v_tile,
                                  o_buffer[i, i_q_h], l_buffer[i, i_q_h],
                                  m_buffer[i, i_q_h], ...,
                                  tile_mask=cur_mask,
                                  use_causal_mask=False,
                                  initialize=large_k_tile_idx == 0, ...)

The outer loop is a sequential_range because each tile updates the accumulators that the next tile reads. The query tiles and query heads inside it are independent, so they use affine_range, which lets the compiler reorder and overlap them.

The cached context length must be a multiple of LARGE_TILE_SZ, and the number of blocks in a tile must be a power of two. The caller must pad the block table to meet these conditions, and the mask hides the padded positions.

Reading blocks with vectorized DMA

Loading a tile means gathering up to LARGE_TILE_SZ / block_size blocks that can sit anywhere in the cache. The kernel turns this gather into indirect DMA loads that use the block table as the index.

First, load_block_tables copies the block table from HBM into SBUF, reshaped to one row per tile. Then transform_block_tables_for_indirect_load prepares the indices for the loads. It folds the KV head into the block index, because the cache is flattened to three dimensions, and it transposes the table so that the block indices for a tile lie along the 128 SBUF partitions:

if num_head > 1:
    # fuse num_block and num_head dimension
    block_tables_partition = block_tables_partition * num_head + head_id

A single load then fetches one block per partition:

loaded = nl.load(kv_cache[0, block_tables[load_idx, i_p, large_k_tile_idx], i_f])

The DMA engines reach full parallelism when a load spans all 128 partitions. When a tile has fewer than 128 blocks, for example 2,048 tokens in blocks of 32 tokens gives 64 blocks, the kernel splits each block into block_size_tiling_factor smaller pieces so that one load still covers 128 partitions:

if num_blocks_per_large_tile < B_P_SIZE:
    block_size_tiling_factor = B_P_SIZE // num_blocks_per_large_tile
    assert block_size % block_size_tiling_factor == 0
else:
    block_size_tiling_factor = 1
tiled_block_size = block_size // block_size_tiling_factor

This split changes the order in which tokens arrive in SBUF. The tensor engine consumes a tile column by column, so after the split it visits tokens with a stride instead of in sequence. The host-side helper reorder_context_mask transposes the context part of the mask to the same order. The caller must apply it before launching the kernel, or the mask and the keys refer to different tokens.

Keys are loaded with tokens on the partitions and then transposed with nl.transpose, because the Q @ K^T matmul needs the head dimension on the partitions. Values stay in the loaded layout, which already matches the P @ V matmul.

Online softmax

_flash_attention_core processes one 128-token query tile against one key tile with the online softmax of FlashAttention. Each query row keeps three accumulators in SBUF: the running maximum score m_buffer, the log of the running softmax denominator l_buffer, and the unnormalized output o_buffer.

For each key tile, the core computes the scores in 512-column pieces and replaces masked positions with a large negative constant:

qk_res_buf[:, k_i_b_f_slice] = nl.where(
    tile_mask[:, k_i_b_f_slice],
    qk_psum[:, nl.ds(0, B_F_SIZE)],
    -9984.0,
    dtype=acc_type,
)

It then takes the new row maximum, rescales the previous output by exp(m_previous - m_current), computes exp(score - m_current) with a fused activation and row sum, multiplies by V, and adds the result to the output. The log-denominator is updated in log space:

l_exp = nl.add(nl.exp(nl.subtract(l_prev, m_current)), ps)
l_buffer[:, 0] = nl.add(m_current, nl.log(l_exp))

After both passes, the kernel normalizes the output once per query tile:

out = nl.multiply(o_buffer[i, i_q_h],
                  nl.exp(m_buffer[i, i_q_h] - l_buffer[i, i_q_h]),
                  dtype=kernel_dtype)

Because the accumulators carry the full softmax state, the order of the tiles does not change the result. The cached context can come first and the new tokens last.

With mixed_precision=True, the matmuls run in BF16 and the scores, maxima and sums accumulate in FP32.

Skipping work in the causal pass

In the second pass, the new tokens attend to each other causally. The core skips a 512-column piece of the score matrix entirely when every key in it comes after every query in the tile:

if use_causal_mask:
    multiplication_required_selection = (q_tile_idx * B_P_SIZE
                                         >= k_i * B_F_SIZE)

Skipped pieces are filled with the large negative constant without a matmul. For a long prefill this removes up to half of the score computation in the second pass. The mask still handles the diagonal pieces and the boundaries between requests.

Writing the new tokens to the cache

The attention kernel reads the cache but does not write to it. A separate function, reshape_and_cache, writes the keys and values of the new tokens. vLLM gives each new token a slot number in slot_mapping. The block is the slot divided by the block size, and the offset within the block is the remainder:

block_indices = torch.div(slot_mapping, block_size, rounding_mode="floor")
block_offsets = slot_mapping % block_size
head_indices = torch.arange(n_kv_head, device=key.device)

kv_cache.index_put_(
    (torch.tensor([0], device=key.device), block_indices[:, None],
     head_indices[None, :], block_offsets[:, None]), key)

The same call with index 1 writes the values. This function is plain PyTorch, not an NKI kernel.

How serving features map onto the kernel

Prefix caching. When requests share a prefix, the scheduler points their block tables at the same physical blocks. The kernel only sees block indices and a mask, so shared blocks need no special handling.

Chunked prefill. A prompt that is split into chunks reaches the kernel as a sequence of steps. In each step, the chunk’s tokens are the new tokens and the earlier chunks are cached blocks. Decode tokens from other requests can share the same step, since each request is a range of rows and columns in the mask.

Grouped-query attention. The grid runs over KV heads, and each program reuses one loaded key and value tile for all the query heads that share it.

References

  • nki_flash_attn.py in vLLM
  • Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention (Kwon et al., 2023)
  • FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness (Dao et al., 2022)

entry.title: EKS Cluster Setup for Trn1 Multi-Node Workloads
entry.summary: A development setup for multi-node Trn1 workloads on EKS, using long-running MPIJob pods, a shared FSx volume and rsync from a laptop, so that a code change does not need a new container image.
entry.content:
A multi-node job on Trn1 instances under EKS can run as an MPI job, with one launcher process that starts the work on every node. If the job runs a fixed command from the container image, each code change needs a new image, a push to the registry and a new deployment. The setup below keeps the pods running between changes. Testing a change then takes only a file sync and an mpirun command.

Cluster layout

The cluster has three parts:

  • Trn1 worker nodes run the model. Each worker pod requests the Neuron devices and EFA interfaces of its node.
  • A launcher pod runs mpirun, which starts the processes on the workers. It needs no accelerator, so it can run on a CPU node.
  • A shared FSx for Lustre volume holds code, checkpoints and logs. Every pod mounts it at /shared, and its contents survive pod restarts. The FSx for Lustre CSI driver provides the volume to the pods.

The Neuron device plugin registers two resources. aws.amazon.com/neuron allocates whole Neuron devices, and aws.amazon.com/neuroncore allocates single NeuronCores. The EFA device plugin registers EFA interfaces as vpc.amazonaws.com/efa. A trn1.32xlarge has 16 Neuron devices and 8 EFA devices, and a trn1n.32xlarge has 16 EFA devices. A worker pod that uses a whole trn1.32xlarge requests 16 and 8.

EFA traffic between nodes needs a security group that allows all traffic between its members, as the Neuron multi-node setup guide describes. The worker node group uses that security group.

The MPI operator

The Kubeflow MPI operator runs an MPIJob as one launcher and a set of workers. With the v2beta1 API and Open MPI, the operator does the following:

  • It creates the worker pods and a headless Service, so each worker has a stable host name.
  • It writes a hostfile that lists the workers into a ConfigMap. It mounts the hostfile in the launcher at /etc/mpi/hostfile and sets OMPI_MCA_orte_default_hostfile, so mpirun finds the workers without a --hostfile flag.
  • It generates an SSH key pair, stores it in a Secret and mounts it at /root/.ssh in every pod. mpirun reaches the workers over SSH, so each worker container must run an SSH server.
  • With launcherCreationPolicy: WaitForWorkersReady, it creates the launcher only after every worker is ready. The default, AtStartup, creates the launcher at once.

The parts of the spec that change between experiments are the launcher command, the worker command and the number of workers:

apiVersion: kubeflow.org/v2beta1
kind: MPIJob
metadata:
  name: trn1-job
spec:
  slotsPerWorker: 1
  launcherCreationPolicy: WaitForWorkersReady
  mpiReplicaSpecs:
    Launcher:
      replicas: 1
      template:
        spec:
          containers:
            - name: launcher
              image: <inference image>
              command: ["mpirun", "--allow-run-as-root", "-np", "2", "python3", "/shared/run.py"]
    Worker:
      replicas: 2
      template:
        spec:
          containers:
            - name: worker
              image: <inference image>
              command: ["bash", "-c", "mkdir -p /run/sshd && /usr/sbin/sshd -De"]
              resources:
                limits:
                  aws.amazon.com/neuron: 16
                  vpc.amazonaws.com/efa: 8

The worker runs sshd in the foreground (-D) and logs to stderr (-e). Debian and Ubuntu builds of sshd refuse to start without the /run/sshd directory, which a container does not create on its own. The operator’s example job also runs sshd -De as its worker command. The full spec also sets the FSx volume mount and the node selectors.

Long-running pods for development

For development, the launcher command becomes sleep infinity. The workers already run sshd, which keeps them alive. All pods stay up until the job is deleted, and code runs in them interactively:

metadata:
  name: <user>-dev
spec:
  slotsPerWorker: 1
  mpiReplicaSpecs:
    Launcher:
      replicas: 1
      template:
        spec:
          containers:
            - name: launcher
              command: ["sleep", "infinity"]
    Worker:
      replicas: 2
      template:
        spec:
          containers:
            - name: worker
              command: ["bash", "-c", "mkdir -p /run/sshd && /usr/sbin/sshd -De"]

On a shared cluster, a user-name prefix on the job name gives each developer a separate job. The operator labels every pod with the job name and its role, and those labels select the pods:

kubectl apply -f dev.yaml
kubectl get pods -l training.kubeflow.org/job-name=<user>-dev

LAUNCHER=$(kubectl get pods -o name \
  -l training.kubeflow.org/job-name=<user>-dev,training.kubeflow.org/job-role=launcher)
kubectl exec -it "$LAUNCHER" -- bash

Running code across the workers

Inside the launcher, mpirun reads the hostfile and connects to the workers over SSH. With one slot per worker, -np 2 starts one process on each of the two workers:

mpirun --allow-run-as-root -np 2 hostname

The code under development lives on the shared volume. The -x option of Open MPI’s mpirun exports an environment variable from the launcher to every process:

export PYTHONPATH=/shared/<user>/src:$PYTHONPATH
mpirun --allow-run-as-root -np 2 -x PYTHONPATH python3 /shared/<user>/run.py

Without -x PYTHONPATH, the worker processes use the image’s default PYTHONPATH. They then import the package installed in the image instead of the working copy on /shared.

Syncing code from a laptop

rsync can use kubectl exec as its remote shell, so edits on a laptop reach a pod without exposing an SSH server outside the cluster. The krsync script from a Server Fault answer wraps this. The pod needs the rsync binary, which many images lack. On a Debian or Ubuntu image, the launcher installs it with:

apt-get update && apt-get install -y rsync

Putting this step in the launcher command avoids repeating it after every restart. A short script syncs a directory to the shared volume through the launcher pod:

# sync.sh
pod=$(kubectl get pods -o name \
  -l training.kubeflow.org/job-name=<user>-dev,training.kubeflow.org/job-role=launcher)
pod=${pod#pod/}
./krsync.sh -a ~/work/src/ "$pod":/shared/<user>/src/

Running the script in a loop keeps the pod’s copy within a few seconds of the laptop:

while true; do ./sync.sh; sleep 1; done > sync.log 2>&1 &

The files land on FSx, so the workers see them as soon as the launcher does.

A separate pod for the AWS CLI

Downloading a checkpoint from S3 needs the AWS CLI, and the inference image may not include it. A small pod that runs the public amazon/aws-cli image and mounts the same FSx volume handles these transfers without changing the inference image:

apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: aws-cli
spec:
  serviceAccountName: <account with S3 access>
  containers:
    - name: aws-cli
      image: amazon/aws-cli
      command: ["sleep", "infinity"]
      volumeMounts:
        - name: fsx
          mountPath: /shared
  volumes:
    - name: fsx
      persistentVolumeClaim:
        claimName: <fsx claim>

The service account maps to an IAM role with read access to the bucket, through IAM roles for service accounts. A file that this pod copies into /shared is visible to the launcher and the workers.

The development loop

A working session with this setup has six steps:

  1. Apply the development job and wait for the pods to reach Running.
  2. Start the sync loop on the laptop.
  3. Open a shell in the launcher pod.
  4. Run the test with mpirun ... -x PYTHONPATH.
  5. Edit on the laptop, wait for the sync, and run the same command again.
  6. Delete the job with kubectl delete mpijob <user>-dev at the end of the session to release the Trn1 nodes.

A new image is needed only when the dependencies change.

References

  • Kubeflow MPI operator, v0.6.0
  • Neuron device plugin for Kubernetes
  • Neuron Kubernetes prerequisites
  • Setting up Trn1 for multi-node execution
  • EFA device plugin for EKS
  • FSx for Lustre CSI driver
  • Open MPI 4.1 mpirun manual
  • IAM roles for service accounts
  • rsync files to a Kubernetes pod (Server Fault)

entry.title: A Simple Tensor Comparison Utility for Accuracy Debugging
entry.summary: A small utility for comparing two tensors during accuracy debugging. It reports the maximum, mean and spread of the difference, checks argmax and top-K agreement, and writes per-layer results to CSV.
entry.content:
When two tensors that are expected to match do not, the investigation should establish the size of the worst and the typical difference, whether the argmax agrees, and whether sampling from each distribution gives the same result. The utility below answers each of these questions.

The utility is most useful in numerics debugging. Typical cases include comparing logits between hardware paths, validating quantization, and checking a kernel against a reference. It serves as the next step when torch.allclose returns False and the cause of the mismatch is unknown.

The comparator

import torch
import csv
from datetime import datetime, timezone


def compare_logits(first: torch.Tensor, second: torch.Tensor, name: str):
    """Compare two tensors element-wise. Prints summary stats and argmax agreement."""
    diff = torch.abs(first - second)
    max_diff = diff.max()
    min_diff = diff.min()
    avg_diff = diff.mean()
    stddev = diff.std()

    first_min, first_max = first.min(), first.max()
    second_min, second_max = second.min(), second.max()

    print(f"{name.upper()}: "
          f"max_diff={max_diff:.5f}, min_diff={min_diff:.5f}, "
          f"avg_diff={avg_diff:.5f}, stddev={stddev:.5f}, "
          f"first range=[{first_min:.5f}, {first_max:.5f}], "
          f"second range=[{second_min:.5f}, {second_max:.5f}]")
    print(f"ArgMax first={torch.argmax(first)}, second={torch.argmax(second)}")

A typical call:

compare_logits(cpu_logits, neuron_logits, "fp32-vs-bf16-bf-decode-step-0")

Output:

FP32-VS-BF16-BF-DECODE-STEP-0: max_diff=0.13281, min_diff=0.00000,
avg_diff=0.00742, stddev=0.01089, first range=[-20.3125, 18.5000],
second range=[-20.4063, 18.5000]
ArgMax first=842, second=842

Each value has the following interpretation:

  • max_diff is the largest element-wise difference. Near a logit value of 18, one BF16 ULP is 0.125. The value of 0.13281 here is just over one ULP, which is acceptable for BF16.
  • avg_diff is the typical difference. When it is much smaller than max_diff, a few outliers account for the worst case.
  • stddev is the spread of the differences. For spread-out rounding noise, the standard deviation of the absolute difference is close to the mean. A standard deviation several times the mean indicates that the error is concentrated in a few elements.
  • Argmax agreement indicates whether greedy decoding selects the same token. If the argmax differs, the generated output will differ. torch.argmax without a dim argument returns an index into the flattened tensor, so the check applies to the logits of a single step.

Top-K sampling check

When generation uses top-K sampling instead of greedy decoding, the sampled tokens should also be compared:

def printTop(next_token_scores, name, top_k=5, seed=0):
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    topk_values, topk_indices = torch.topk(next_token_scores, top_k)
    probs = torch.nn.functional.softmax(topk_values, dim=-1)

    inputs_in_topk = torch.multinomial(probs, num_samples=1, replacement=True)
    inputs = torch.gather(topk_indices, 0, inputs_in_topk)
    print(f"TopK-{top_k} for {name}: {inputs}")

# inside compare_logits, optionally:
printTop(first, "first")
printTop(second, "second")

This function samples one token from the top-K distribution of each tensor. Both calls use the same seed, so identical distributions produce the same token. If the argmax agrees but the sampled tokens differ for several seeds, the two distributions differ in shape even though their peaks match.

Bulk comparison with CSV output

Comparing many tensors at once, such as the output of every layer, calls for a version that writes a CSV file:

def write_to_csv(results, filename=None):
    csv_headers = ["Param", "Max Diff", "Min Diff", "Mean Diff", "Std. Dev Diff"]
    if filename is None:
        ts = datetime.now(timezone.utc).strftime('%Y%m%dT%H%M%S')
        filename = f"tensor-diffs-{ts}.csv"

    with open(filename, 'w', newline='') as f:
        writer = csv.writer(f)
        writer.writerow(csv_headers)
        for row in results:
            writer.writerow(row)


def get_statistics(name: str, bf16: torch.Tensor, fp32: torch.Tensor):
    """Compute summary statistics for one bf16 vs fp32 comparison and return the CSV row."""
    print(f"\n{name} ...")
    diff = torch.abs(bf16 - fp32)
    mean_diff = torch.mean(diff)
    std_diff = torch.std(diff)
    max_diff = torch.max(diff)
    min_diff = torch.min(diff)

    print(f"  Max_diff: {max_diff}, Min_diff: {min_diff}, "
          f"Mean_diff: {mean_diff}, StdDev: {std_diff}")

    return [name, max_diff.item(), min_diff.item(), mean_diff.item(), std_diff.item()]

A typical loop over layers:

def compare_tensors():
    layer_count = 32
    results = []
    for layer_idx in range(layer_count):
        bf16 = torch.load(f'/tmp/bf16_layer_{layer_idx}_out.pt')
        fp32 = torch.load(f'/tmp/fp32_layer_{layer_idx}_out.pt')
        results.append(get_statistics(f'layer_{layer_idx}_out', bf16, fp32))

    write_to_csv(results)

Output CSV:

Param,Max Diff,Min Diff,Mean Diff,Std. Dev Diff
layer_0_out,0.0078125,0.0,0.001234,0.000874
layer_1_out,0.0107422,0.0,0.002145,0.001231
layer_2_out,0.0146484,0.0,0.003012,0.001682
...

Plotting these columns shows how the error grows from layer to layer, and the shape of the curve usually indicates the cause:

  • Gradual, steady growth is expected. Each layer adds its own BF16 rounding error to the residual stream.
  • A sudden jump or rapid growth indicates a bug. Some operation amplifies the error instead of allowing it to dissipate, and the first layer with the jump is where to look.
  • Flat or very slow growth indicates that the implementation limits error accumulation, for example by accumulating matrix multiplications or collectives in FP32.

Use cases

The utility applies to three common debugging scenarios.

Quantization validation. A model is cast from BF16 to FP8, and the per-layer outputs of the two versions are compared. The CSV records the error that each layer adds, which shows whether the quantization is too lossy.

Cross-hardware comparison. The same model runs on GPU and on Neuron, and the logits are saved after each batch and compared. A layer with a much larger difference than the others is the first candidate for investigation.

Kernel validation. The output of a new NKI kernel is compared against a PyTorch reference. A mismatched argmax at a step where the top token clearly leads indicates incorrect math. A large max_diff with a matching argmax indicates correct math with numeric inaccuracy.

The utility deliberately omits plotting, tolerance settings and a pass/fail verdict. The appropriate tolerance depends on the use case, so that decision belongs to the caller.

Limitations

  • Whether the difference matters for the model’s output. Two outputs can differ by 5% and still sample the same token. Two others can differ by 0.1% and produce different sequences, when that small difference falls on a step where the top two tokens are nearly tied. The utility measures numeric similarity, not behavioral similarity.
  • Where the divergence started. Locating the first divergent layer requires calling the utility at several layer boundaries.
  • Whether the difference is structured. A max_diff of 0.1 can come from a single outlier or from a uniform 0.1 offset across the tensor. The standard deviation offers a hint, and a histogram provides a definitive answer.

entry.title: Neuron - Handling NaNs
entry.summary: A runbook for triaging Neuron accuracy issues and means to verify the model accuracy
entry.content:
LLMs work with floating point numbers and susceptible to saturation or loss of precision issue. This is typically seen with NaN (Not a Number) errors.

Neuron compiler suggests the following options to overcome the NaN issue.

Compiler flag: --enable-saturate-infinity

Ref A computation that can generate +/- infinity is at a high risk of generating Not-a-Number (NaN) values when the infinity value is used in subsequent computations. This option helps avoid this by converting +Inf/-Inf values to MAX/MIN_FLOAT before operations that could produce NaN values for +Inf/-Inf inputs on the target architecture. While this option helps to avoid NaN values, there is a potential performance degradation that occurs during model execution when this conversion is enabled.

Compiler flag: --enable-mixed-precision-accumulation

Ref To perform intermediate calculations of reduction operators (such as the dot or reduce operators) in FP32 regardless of the operation’s defined datatype.

NaNs due to saturation

To triage an intermediate BF16 tensor, np.isnan would not work, since NumPy supports only float16, float32, and float64 by default and bfloat16 is not a standard NumPy dtype. The data typically looks like bf16_hex = [0x3f80, 0xbf80, 0x4000, 0x7f80, 0xff80, 0x7fc0]. We can either try to use torch.isnan or convert to fp32 as below.

Convert to fp32 for printing/checking

def bf16_to_float32(bits):
    import struct
    # Pad with 16 zero bits to match float32
    f32_bits = bits << 16
    return struct.unpack('f', struct.pack('I', f32_bits))[0]

converted = [bf16_to_float32(b) for b in bf16_hex]
print(converted)

To add Neuron available conversion method

entry.title: AI Compilers - A Study guide
entry.summary: A growing list/study guide of AI compilers, from foundational concepts like graph lowering and systolic arrays to practical tools like TorchDynamo and Glow.
entry.content:
The following formulates a study guide for learning about AI compilers and systematically understanding the inner functions. These are targetted more towards Model and Framework level developers to build a deeper understanding of compiler functions.

AI Compilers Demystified - An Introduction

Medium Article is a good high level summary of where AI compiler interacts with the frameworks and no learning about ML Accelerators is complete without learning about Systolic Arrays.

Ref: https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.03794

ML Systems for TinyML

HW Acceleration provides an excellent end to end context on why ML compilers are necessary for compute optimization and the evolution of TPUs to ASICs. CS249R is a good course for edgeML learning, but necessarily for compilers only.

Glow: Graph Lowering Compiler Techniques for Neural Networks

The Glow paper discusses what is compilation and how optimized code is generated for different types of hardware and what IR (Intermediate representations) are. Though its outdated and replaced with TorchDynamo and TorchInductor, this paper sets up a good fundamental framework for understanding the inner mechanisms.

Textbook - Deeplearningsystems.ai

A no-nonsense rich end-to-end textbook to understand the fundamentals of DL algorithms (Chapters 1-6) and Hardware and compiler level optimizations for these algorithms (Chapters 7-9)

A simple compiler Example

Build a Hardware Compiler for Machine Learning and Image Processing walks through in 10 minutes the concepts of building an Hardware accelerator for Image processing and ML algorithms using frameworks like Halide and others. The goal is to convert architecture-agnostic algorithm descriptions into hardware accelerators. It emphasizes using High-Level Synthesis (HLS) as a backend instead of directly targeting Verilog or VHDL. HLS allows compilers to emit HLS C++ code with directives, enhancing productivity despite potentially sacrificing some control over optimization. It goes into some of the design choices of handling optimizations affecting program semantics (e.g., quantization, bit width tuning) at the frontend which ensures optimizations directly impacting program outputs are addressed early in the compilation process. They utilize “for loops” as an intermediate representation and as a target output for HLS. Frameworks like TensorFlow, PyTorch, Halide, and TVM naturally express algorithms as dense linear algebra operations, simplifying translation to HLS-compatible constructs. They discuss loop transformations (e.g., fusion, unrolling) and memory optimizations (e.g., banking).

A day in the life of a Compiler Engineer

Torchdynamo deep dive gives the viewer an idea on what issues does a Framework and compiler engineer faces during their development cycle. Edward from the PyTorch team discuss TorchDynamo, graph capture part of the torch.compile ecosystem which aims to capture Python code efficiently by capturing operations in a format suitable for compilation. TorchDynamo intercepts Python bytecode execution to generate and optimize computation graphs.He deep dives into bailouts in deep learning compilers and optimizations in symbolic evaluation during graph capture.

Platforms for AI accelerator design

A concept platform for designing and evaluating ML Accelerators - Gemmini | Tutorial. An interesting read to understand what bottlenecks usually occur in accelerator design and challenges in designing generalized hardware.

References for further readings/courses

  1. Textbook: Efficient Processing of Deep Neural Networks by Vivienne Sze, Yu-Hsin Chen, Tien-Ju Yang and Joel S. Emer
  2. A survey of papers and books about ML Accelerators
  3. EE290-2 - Hardware for ML from Berkeley
  4. ECE 5545: Machine Learning Hardware and Systems - Well detailed course for ML HW and Systems design with Course Videos
  5. C4ML Course
  6. WashU-cse548
  7. IOC5009 - Accelerator Architectures for Machine Learning

Other Compiler implementations

  1. AutoKernel
  2. NNVM

entry.title: AWS Neuron SDK, an Overview and Glossary
entry.summary: An overview of the AWS Neuron SDK for Inferentia and Trainium, followed by a glossary of the hardware, compiler and systems terms that come up when working on the Neuron stack.
entry.content:
AWS Neuron is the software development kit (SDK) for running deep learning and generative AI workloads on Amazon EC2 instances built on AWS Inferentia and AWS Trainium. It integrates with PyTorch and TensorFlow, so models written in those frameworks can be compiled, trained and deployed on Neuron hardware with few code changes.

Neuron SDK components

Neuron Compiler. The compiler translates a model from the framework’s graph representation into a Neuron Executable File Format (NEFF) file, which contains code optimized for Inferentia and Trainium.

Neuron Runtime. The runtime loads NEFF files onto the NeuronCores, manages device memory, and executes the compiled models.

Framework integrations. Libraries such as torch-neuronx, transformers-neuronx and NeuronX Distributed connect the frameworks to the compiler and runtime, and provide model-parallel building blocks for large models.

Developer tools. Tools such as neuron-top, neuron-monitor and neuron-profile report device utilization, and profile and debug compiled models.

Inference performance techniques

Neuron applies several techniques to improve inference performance:

  • Batching processes multiple inputs together to raise throughput, which suits cost-sensitive workloads.
  • Pipelining splits a model across multiple NeuronCores so that each core holds part of the model’s weights on chip. This reduces data movement for latency-sensitive workloads.
  • Overlapping operations run independent work concurrently, such as loading data while computing, so that the hardware spends less time idle.
  • Operator fusion combines several operations into one, which reduces intermediate memory traffic.
  • Quantization lowers the precision of weights and activations to reduce memory use and increase speed, usually with a small loss in accuracy.
  • Speculative decoding uses a small draft model to propose several tokens, which the large model then verifies in a single pass.
  • Custom C++ operators implement operations that the compiler does not handle well, for specific model components.

Glossary

The following terms come up frequently when working on the Neuron stack.

Hardware

FPGA (Field-Programmable Gate Array). An FPGA contains a fabric of programmable logic blocks that can be configured after manufacturing to perform specific tasks. A GPU has a fixed design. This flexibility makes FPGAs common in cryptography, financial modeling and high-frequency trading.

ASIC (Application-Specific Integrated Circuit). An ASIC is a chip designed for one purpose, and its hardware is optimized for that task. Inferentia and Trainium are ASICs designed for deep learning inference and training.

PCIe (Peripheral Component Interconnect Express). PCIe is a high-speed interface standard that connects devices such as GPUs, accelerators, network cards and NVMe storage to the CPU and memory. Each device connects through a point-to-point link made of one or more lanes, which a root complex or PCIe switch routes. Devices can also transfer data directly to each other through peer-to-peer transfers.

Memory-Mapped I/O (MMIO). With MMIO, a device’s registers and memory appear at specific addresses in the CPU’s address space. The CPU communicates with the device using ordinary load and store instructions instead of special I/O instructions.

Performance

Arithmetic intensity. Arithmetic intensity is the ratio of computation, measured in floating-point operations (FLOPs), to data movement, measured in bytes. It indicates whether an operation is compute-bound or memory-bound. For example, applying ReLU to a BF16 tensor reads 2 bytes, performs 1 comparison and writes 2 bytes per element, which gives an arithmetic intensity of 1 FLOP per 4 bytes. At such a low ratio, memory access takes longer than computation, so the operation is memory-bound (reference).

Gradient checkpointing (activation checkpointing). Gradient checkpointing reduces memory use by discarding the activations of selected layers during the forward pass and recomputing them during the backward pass. It trades extra computation for lower memory use. For a checkpointed module, only the module’s inputs and outputs stay in memory after the forward pass (reference).

Compiler optimizations

Strength reduction replaces an expensive operation with an equivalent cheaper one, for example replacing multiplication by a power of two with a bit shift.

Constant folding evaluates constant expressions at compile time and replaces them with their values.

Common subexpression elimination computes a repeated expression once and reuses the result.

Dead-code elimination removes code that does not affect the program’s output, such as computations whose results are never used.

Scalar replacement replaces array references with scalar variables where possible, which reduces memory accesses.

If-conversion turns conditional branches into predicated or conditional instructions, which removes branch penalties and exposes more instruction-level parallelism.

Function inlining replaces a function call with the body of the function, which removes the call overhead and enables further optimization.

Call specialization creates a specialized version of a function for arguments known at compile time.

Peephole optimization examines a small window of consecutive instructions and replaces inefficient sequences with faster ones.

Loop canonicalization rewrites loops to start at index 0 and step by 1, which simplifies analysis and enables further loop optimizations.

Constant generation replaces index calculations with precomputed constants.

Load/store elimination removes redundant pairs of loads and stores to the same memory location.

Compiler frameworks

XLA (Accelerated Linear Algebra). XLA is a domain-specific compiler for linear algebra that optimizes machine learning computations for accelerators. It originated in TensorFlow and also serves JAX and PyTorch through PyTorch/XLA. The Neuron PyTorch integration builds on PyTorch/XLA.

TVM. TVM is an open-source deep learning compiler stack that optimizes models for many hardware targets, including CPUs, GPUs and specialized accelerators.

MLIR (Multi-Level Intermediate Representation). MLIR is a compiler infrastructure for defining intermediate representations at several levels of abstraction. It lets compilers share optimizations and lower programs step by step toward different hardware.

LLVM and GCC. LLVM is a modular compiler infrastructure built from reusable libraries around a common intermediate representation (IR). Many compilers for GPUs and accelerators use LLVM as their back end because its components are easy to reuse. GCC is a compiler collection with a long history in production systems, and it supports a very wide range of CPU architectures. LLVM’s library design makes it easier to embed in other tools.

Virtualization

Hypervisor. A hypervisor creates and runs virtual machines. A Type 1 (bare-metal) hypervisor runs directly on the hardware and provides strong isolation and performance, for example VMware ESXi, Microsoft Hyper-V, Xen and the AWS Nitro Hypervisor. A Type 2 (hosted) hypervisor runs on a host operating system, for example VMware Workstation and Oracle VirtualBox.

SR-IOV (Single Root I/O Virtualization). SR-IOV lets one physical PCIe device, such as a network card, appear as several separate devices. The device exposes a physical function (PF) and multiple virtual functions (VFs). The hypervisor assigns VFs directly to virtual machines, which then access the device with near-native performance and little virtualization overhead.

For more detail, see the AWS Neuron documentation.
